Rear fog light
The rear fog light is on — a bright red light at the rear.
Use it only in fog, snow or heavy rain. Turn it off in clear weather: it dazzles drivers behind you and makes your brake lights harder to see.
Electric parking brake
A fault in the electric parking brake (EPB): it may not apply or may not release.
When parked, play it safe: leave it in gear or in P, and chock a wheel on a slope.
Switch the engine off and restart: after a voltage dip the fault sometimes clears. Check the battery.
If it stays, it needs a diagnosis: the code will show whether it’s the caliper motor, a wire or the switch.
Key not detected
The car can’t find the smart key inside. The engine won’t stall while driving, but it may not restart once you stop.
Make sure the key is in the car. Keep it away from your phone, other keys and metal — they interfere with the signal.
Hold the key right against the Start button and press it: many cars will start this way even with a dead key battery.
Replace the key battery. If that doesn’t help, try the spare key.
Key battery low
The key battery is almost dead — soon the car won’t be able to detect the key.
Replace the battery: usually a CR2032 or CR2025 — the type is printed on the battery itself.
Until you replace it, start the car by holding the key right against the Start button.

Steering lock (ESCL)
The electronic steering column lock is faulty: the steering may not unlock, and the car won’t start.
Rock the steering wheel left and right while pressing Start or turning the key — the lock may be stuck.
Check the battery: with low voltage the steering lock often doesn’t work.
If it keeps happening, the steering lock and its power supply need a diagnosis.
Warning
The triangle with “!” comes on with a message on the instrument cluster display that says what’s wrong. On Toyota and Lexus it’s red.
Read the message on the cluster display and look it up in the owner’s manual. Many cars keep past messages in the cluster menu.
If a red symbol is also on or the car behaves oddly, stop and find out why.
If there’s no message but the symbol stays on, it needs a scan tool diagnosis.

The control unit has limited power to protect the engine, transmission or hybrid battery. The car drives but accelerates poorly.
Drive gently, with no passing or hard acceleration, and get to a shop.
Hybrid or EV: the symbol can come on when the battery is nearly empty, overheated or very cold. Charge it or wait.
If it doesn’t go away, read the trouble codes with a scan tool: they’ll show the cause.

Rear window defroster
The rear window defroster is on. It usually switches itself off after 10–20 minutes.
If the glass doesn’t clear or clears in stripes, check the heating grid lines and the contacts at the edges of the glass: they often get torn off.
If it doesn’t heat at all, check the defroster fuse and relay.
Passenger airbag off
The front passenger airbag is switched off. That’s correct when a rear-facing child seat is in the front seat.
If an adult is sitting there and the symbol is on, check the airbag switch: it’s usually key-operated, on the end of the dashboard or in the glove box.
If the airbag switches itself off with an adult passenger, the seat occupant sensor needs a diagnosis.
Ice warning
It’s about +3 °C or colder outside: the road may be icy, especially on bridges and in the shade.
Slow down, leave more following distance and brake early and gently.
AWD/4WD fault
The AWD control unit has found a fault or the coupling has overheated: the car may drive on one axle only. The same symbol in green just means 4WD is engaged.
Don’t spin the wheels. Stop, let the coupling cool for 10–15 minutes and restart.
Check that all four tires match: different sizes or uneven wear upset the drive system.
If it stays on, it needs a diagnosis: common culprits are a wheel speed sensor, the coupling or the mode switch.
Differential lock
The differential lock is on: the wheels on the axle turn together. It’s only for off-road and slippery ground.
Turn the lock off on pavement: with it the vehicle turns poorly and the tires and drivetrain wear faster.
If the symbol flashes, the lock hasn’t engaged or disengaged yet. Drive slowly straight ahead; if that doesn’t help, check the lock sensor and actuator.
Air suspension
An air suspension fault: the vehicle may sag or not hold its ride height.
If the vehicle has sagged, don’t drive fast or over rough roads: you can damage the suspension and the underbody.
Start the engine and wait a few minutes: the compressor should raise the body. If it doesn’t, check the compressor fuse and relay.
If it sags overnight, air is leaking somewhere: an air spring, the lines or the valves. It needs a diagnosis.
Start-stop unavailable
The start-stop system is switched off with its button, temporarily unavailable or faulty. You can keep driving.
The system won’t stop the engine until the battery is charged and the engine is warm, or while strong heating or A/C is on — that’s normal.
If the symbol stays on all the time, check the battery. Start-stop cars use AGM or EFB batteries, and a new one often has to be registered with a scan tool.
If that doesn’t help, it needs a diagnosis: often the battery sensor on the negative terminal is at fault.
The engine air filter is clogged: the engine is short of air, power drops and fuel use goes up.
Replace the air filter and log it in the “Maintenance” section.
If the filter is new but the light stays on, check the restriction (vacuum) sensor on the filter housing and its connector.
Power take-off (PTO)
The PTO is engaged: the engine is driving the pump of the dump body, crane or other equipment.
Disengage the PTO before driving off unless the owner’s manual allows driving with it engaged.
If you’ve disengaged it but the symbol stays on, check the PTO engagement sensor and its wire.
Trailer ABS/EBS
A trailer ABS or EBS fault: the trailer brakes still work, but the wheels may lock under hard braking.
Brake early and gently, especially on slippery roads and downhill.
Check the ABS/EBS connector between the tractor and trailer (ISO 7638): fully plugged in, contacts not corroded, cable intact.
If it stays on, the trailer needs a diagnosis: often a wheel speed sensor or the modulator power supply.
A turn signal or the hazards are on. If it flashes twice as fast as usual, a turn signal bulb on that side has burned out.
If it flashes fast, find which bulb is out — front, rear or the side repeater on the fender — and replace it.
If it doesn’t flash at all or stays on solid, check the turn signal fuse and flasher relay, and if an alarm is fitted, its wiring.

The start-stop system shut the engine off while you’re stopped to save fuel. That’s normal.
The engine restarts by itself when you release the brake (automatic) or press the clutch (manual). You can turn the system off with the button marked A.
Lane keeping assist
The system watches the lane markings and steers back or warns you if the car drifts out of the lane. A yellow or gray symbol means it can’t see the lines or is off.
If it can’t see the lines, clean the windshield in front of the camera by the mirror. It switches off by itself in snow, rain and on worn markings.
After a windshield replacement, the camera has to be calibrated at a shop.
Hill descent control (HDC)
Hill descent control is on: on a steep downhill the car brakes by itself and holds a low speed.
Flashing on a descent means the system is braking — that’s normal. The brakes may make noise while it works.
Turn the system off with its button on level roads. If it’s yellow, the system is unavailable or faulty.
Auto Hold
Auto Hold is on: after you stop, the car holds the brakes itself, so you can take your foot off the pedal.
To pull away, just press the gas — the brake releases by itself.
If it won’t turn on, check that the driver’s seat belt is buckled and the door is closed: many cars won’t enable it otherwise.
Engine brake / retarder
The engine (exhaust) brake or retarder is on: the truck slows down without wearing the brake linings.
Use it on long downhill grades so the brakes don’t overheat. Engage it carefully on slippery roads: the truck can skid.
If the symbol is on but there’s no braking effect, check the switch, the engine brake solenoid valve and its wiring.

The coolant is still cold. The symbol goes out once the engine warms up.
For the first few minutes drive gently and keep the revs low.

After a crash or a hard hit: the fuel or power safety cutoff has tripped

In a crash, or after hitting a deep pothole, a bump or a curb, the car shuts off the fuel pump for safety — so a damaged fuel line doesn’t start a fire. On some cars a crash also fires a pyrotechnic fuse at the battery and cuts all power. It’s a safety feature, not a fault: if there’s no fuel leak, it can be reset.
Inspect the car first: if you smell gasoline or it’s wet or dripping underneath, don’t turn the pump on and don’t start it — call a tow truck. If the airbags deployed, take it to a mechanic.

The starter cranks but the engine won’t start and you don’t hear the fuel pump prime — find the inertia fuel pump shutoff switch and press its button until it clicks. It’s usually a red or black button on top of a small unit.

Where to look: most often in the front passenger footwell behind the side trim panel or behind the glove box; sometimes under the steering wheel by the pedals behind a panel, under the hood on the firewall, or in the trunk behind the side trim. The exact spot is in the owner’s manual, in the section on the emergency fuel shutoff.

Examples: Ford Focus — on the right under the dash or behind the right side panel in the passenger footwell; Ford Fiesta — in the passenger footwell behind the glove box, on some hatchbacks in the trunk behind the right trim; Ford Transit 2000–2014 and Transit Connect before 2013 — on the left by the pedals behind the lower panel; Transit from 2014, Transit Custom, Transit Connect from 2013 and Transit Courier — behind the glove box; Jaguar — on the left ahead of the door pillar under the dash, behind a trim panel with a finger hole. Some Lada, UAZ and Daewoo cars have one too — check the manual.
After pressing it, turn the ignition off for 10–15 seconds and back on: the pump should hum for 2–3 seconds. Then start the engine.

No button — on many modern cars the control unit itself cuts the pump on a crash signal from the airbag module. Turn the ignition off, open and close the driver’s door, wait a minute and turn it back on. If that doesn’t help, it needs a scan tool: the airbag module keeps a crash record that a mechanic clears, and sometimes the module is replaced.

The car is completely dead, or the starter won’t crank with a charged battery — check the pyrotechnic fuse at the battery positive terminal or in the power fuse box next to it. BMWs with the battery in the trunk have one, for example: after an impact the terminal fires apart, the lights and radio may still work, but the engine won’t start. A fired pyro fuse can’t be reset — it’s replaced, then the airbag codes are cleared with a scan tool.
If the airbags or the pyro fuse fired, or the wiring or fuel lines are damaged, it needs diagnostics: Oleg will check the airbag module, clear the crash records and find what else the impact damaged.
The switch can trip without a crash — from a hard hit into a pothole or a curb, or while loading onto a tow truck. Before hunting for a complex fault, press it: it takes a minute.
If you smell gasoline, don’t press anything and don’t start the engine.
The motorcycle fell and won’t start: the tip-over sensor has tripped
Most fuel-injected motorcycles have a tip-over (bank angle) sensor: when the bike falls, it kills the engine and cuts the fuel pump and ignition to prevent a fire.
If you smell gasoline or fuel is leaking, don’t start it until the leak is fixed.
Stand the motorcycle up on its wheels or stand.
Turn the ignition off for 10–15 seconds and back on: you should hear the fuel pump prime.
Check the engine kill switch on the right handlebar — it often gets knocked in a fall.
Still won’t start — inspect the tip-over sensor connector (usually under the seat) and the fuses, and look for wires broken in the fall.
After a fall, a bike often won’t start because of the handlebar kill switch — check it first.

Automatic shifter in N
Is it an automatic — a conventional automatic, CVT or automated manual? Set the parking brake, press the brake pedal, move the shifter to N and try to start it again.
Automatic: the starter cranks in N
Automatic: silent in N too
Manual transmission
Automatic: no crank in P — start it in N

On an automatic, the starter cranks only in P and N — the transmission range sensor (neutral safety switch, inhibitor) allows it. Its contacts burn and wear over time: in P the starter circuit stops closing, while in N it still closes. That’s why the car often starts in neutral.
Start in N only with the parking brake set and the brake pedal pressed: in neutral the car can roll.
Set the parking brake, press the brake pedal, move the shifter to N and start the engine.
Silent in N too — put the lever back in P, wiggle it slightly within P and try again: a burnt contact sometimes closes with a small shift.
Look at the instrument cluster: does the letter on the display match the lever position? If another letter or none shows in P, the sensor is out of adjustment or the shifter cable has stretched.
If it starts in N, drive as usual. When you leave the car, put the lever in P and set the parking brake.
Won’t start in P or N — check the starter fuse and relay (below) and the range sensor connector on the transmission for corrosion and moisture.
A scan tool may show a range sensor or P/N switch code — for example, P0705 or P0850.

If it starts only in N, have the range sensor checked: over time it will stop allowing a start in N too. It also tells the transmission control unit which gear is selected. Oleg will check the sensor, the shifter cable and the starter interlock circuit, and adjust or replace the sensor.
A common story: on an automatic the starter is silent in P but cranks in N, and the car starts. The range sensor contacts have burnt. You can get to a shop like this, but don’t put off the repair.
Parking brake set, foot on the brake, no one near the car.
Automatic: shift to N and try again — with a burnt range sensor the starter often won’t crank in P but will in N.

The misfires aren’t in just one cylinder: usually the mixture, a vacuum leak, fuel or a shared ignition circuit is to blame.
The last two digits are the cylinder number. Swap the coils or spark plugs with the next cylinder: if the misfire “moves”, that part is to blame.
The last two digits are the cylinder number: the code is about its injector circuit. Check that injector’s connector and coil resistance.
The coil number is the last two digits minus 50: P0351 is coil A, the first one. It usually matches the cylinder number.

The type of failure, a number from 0 to 31: above or below normal, open, short, no data on the network.
